## Overview

`mixedcirc` fits one harmonic regression model per molecular feature. It can
use ordinary linear models for independent observations or mixed-effects
models when measurements are repeated within subjects. The same workflow
handles continuous measurements, RNA-seq counts supplied as an
`edgeR::DGEList`, and paired methylated/unmethylated counts from RRBS or other
bisulfite-sequencing experiments.

The main steps are:

1. prepare a feature matrix and sample metadata;
2. fit feature-wise models with `mixedcirc_detect()`;
3. extract rhythmicity estimates and direct between-group contrasts;
4. adjust for testing many features, inspect fit diagnostics, and visualize
   the results.

This vignette introduces the full workflow and then describes the input routes
for RNA-seq and paired methylation counts.

```{r load-package}
library(mixedcirc)
```

## Data layout

For a numeric matrix or data frame, rows are observations and columns are
features. `meta_input` has one row for each observation, in exactly the same
order. The arguments `time`, `group`, `id`, and `replicate_id` are column names
in this metadata, not vectors supplied separately.

An `edgeR::DGEList` follows the usual RNA-seq convention: genes are rows and
samples are columns. The number and order of its columns must match the rows of
`meta_input`.

RRBS input has a separate paired layout, described below.

## The harmonic model

For period \(\tau\), mixedcirc represents time with

$$
\cos(2\pi t/\tau) \quad\text{and}\quad \sin(2\pi t/\tau).
$$

In a two-group continuous-data analysis, the default fixed part of the model is

$$
y = M_g + C_g\cos(2\pi t/\tau) + S_g\sin(2\pi t/\tau) + \epsilon.
$$

A mixed model can add a subject-specific random intercept, or random intercept
and harmonic terms. The latter allows subjects to differ in mesor and rhythm,
but it requires enough observations per subject to estimate the additional
variance components reliably.

Amplitude and phase are derived from the harmonic coefficients:

$$
A_g = \sqrt{C_g^2 + S_g^2}, \qquad
\phi_g = \operatorname{atan2}(-S_g, C_g).
$$

The fitted curve is \(M_g + A_g\cos(2\pi t/\tau + \phi_g)\).
`mixedcirc_detect()` represents phase on `[-2*pi, 0)`. Peak time is
`-phase / omega`, wrapped into one period, where `omega = 2*pi/period`.
`mixedcirc_detectpeaks()` performs this conversion.

Rhythmicity within a group is a joint test of \(C_g=S_g=0\). A direct
differential-rhythm test compares both harmonic coefficients between groups.
Different significance decisions in two separate within-group tests do not, by
themselves, show that the rhythms differ.

## Continuous repeated-measures analysis

The simulator returns feature measurements, matching metadata, optional
weights, and the generating parameters. Here each subject is observed at eight
times in one of two groups.

```{r continuous-simulation}
sim <- mixedcirc_simulate_data(
  n_subjects_per_group = 4,
  n_timepoints = 8,
  n_features = 5,
  groups = c("control", "treated"),
  seed = 17
)

dim(sim$data_input)
head(sim$meta_input)
```

Use a mixed model because observations from the same subject are correlated.
A random mesor is a practical starting point for modest repeated-measures
studies.

```{r continuous-fit}
fit <- mixedcirc_detect(
  data_input = sim$data_input,
  meta_input = sim$meta_input,
  time = "time",
  group = "group",
  id = "id",
  period = 24,
  lm_method = "lme",
  random_effect_type = "mesor"
)

length(fit)
fit[[1]]@results
```

For independent observations, set `lm_method = "lm"` and
`random_effect_type = "none"`. If `id` is omitted, mixedcirc switches to the
ordinary linear model and reports that change.

### Analysis-ready results

The long result tables are usually more convenient than accessing S4 slots.
Adjusted p-values are calculated across features separately within each group
or contrast.

```{r result-tables}
estimates <- mixedcirc_results(fit, type = "estimates")
contrasts <- mixedcirc_contrasts(fit)
diagnostics <- mixedcirc_results(fit, type = "diagnostics")

head(estimates)
head(contrasts)
mixedcirc_summary(fit)
```

`p_rhythm` tests rhythmicity in one group. `p_differential` is the pairwise
joint test that the two harmonic coefficients differ. With more than two
groups, `p_rhythm_global` asks whether any group is rhythmic, whereas
`p_differential_global` asks whether the harmonic coefficient vector differs
anywhere among the groups.

`mixedcirc_classify()` combines these tests into conservative descriptive
classes. Gain, loss, and altered-rhythm calls require significant direct
evidence of a between-group difference. A feature that crosses the rhythmicity
threshold in only one group but lacks a significant direct contrast is labelled
uncertain. Optional thresholds can require a minimum amplitude change,
peak-time shift, or harmonic distance.

```{r classification}
classes <- mixedcirc_classify(
  fit,
  alpha = 0.05,
  min_amplitude_change = 0.25,
  min_phase_shift = 1
)
head(classes)
```

Classification organizes statistical results; it is not a separate model and
does not replace inspection of estimates, uncertainty, and diagnostics.

### Plots and subject-specific rhythms

An individual fit shows observations and the fitted harmonic curve.

```{r individual-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
plot(fit[[1]])
```

Dataset-level plots show complementary aspects of the analysis.

```{r dataset-plots, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
mixedcirc_plot_heatmap(fit, npoints = 48)
mixedcirc_plot_differential(fit, label_n = 3)
mixedcirc_plot_polar(fit, label_n = 3)
mixedcirc_plot_design(fit, by_subject = TRUE)
```

The polar plot uses angle for peak time and radial distance for amplitude;
transparency indicates whether the within-group rhythmicity test passed the
selected FDR threshold. The differential plot should be interpreted together
with the direct contrast table.

Model diagnostics are available as a table and as residual or quantile plots.

```{r diagnostic-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
mixedcirc_plot_diagnostics(fit, features = colnames(sim$data_input)[1:2])
```

When random harmonic terms were fitted, individual rhythm estimates can be
reconstructed from fixed and random effects.

```{r subject-rhythms}
fit_subject <- mixedcirc_detect(
  sim$data_input[, 1:2, drop = FALSE],
  sim$meta_input,
  time = "time",
  group = "group",
  id = "id",
  random_effect_type = "mesor_phase"
)

head(mixedcirc_subject_rhythms(fit_subject))
```

Check convergence and singularity before interpreting subject-level
amplitudes or phases. A simpler random-intercept model is preferable when the
study cannot support random harmonic coefficients.

## Covariates and linear trends

Additional fixed effects are supplied as a one-sided formula. They must be
columns of `meta_input`.

```{r covariates}
sim_cov <- mixedcirc_simulate_data(
  n_subjects_per_group = 4,
  n_timepoints = 6,
  n_features = 3,
  groups = c("A", "B"),
  include_covariates = TRUE,
  batch_effects = c(B1 = 0, B2 = 2),
  seed = 23
)

fit_cov <- mixedcirc_detect(
  sim_cov$data_input,
  sim_cov$meta_input,
  time = "time",
  group = "group",
  id = "id",
  formula_extra = ~ age + batch
)
```

If a linear time trend is part of the scientific model, it can be estimated
alongside the harmonic terms with `formula_extra = ~ time`. This simultaneous
model is generally preferable for inference to removing a trend first.

Two helpers are available when a separate detrended matrix is genuinely needed:
`mixedcirc_remove_trend()` residualizes the input measurements, whereas
`mixedcirc_detrend()` residualizes the fitted curves stored in a mixedcirc
object. The latter is descriptive post-processing and does not change the
original rhythm tests.

```{r detrending-example, eval=FALSE}
residualized_input <- mixedcirc_remove_trend(
  sim$data_input,
  sim$meta_input,
  time = "time",
  group = "group",
  id = "id"
)

detrended_fitted_curves <- mixedcirc_detrend(fit, per_group = TRUE)
```

## Bootstrap uncertainty

`mixedcirc_boottest()` simulates new responses from one retained fitted model,
refits the model, and recomputes mesor, amplitude, and phase summaries. This is
a parametric bootstrap: subjects and time points are not resampled.

```{r bootstrap, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
boot <- mixedcirc_boottest(
  fit[[1]],
  nsim = 10,
  seed = 31,
  parallel = "no"
)
boot
mixedcirc_plot_bootstrap(boot)
```

Ten replicates keep this vignette quick; a real analysis needs substantially
more. Phase intervals use wrapped deviations around the fitted phase, so an
interval can cross the circular boundary without appearing to span the whole
cycle.

## RNA-seq counts

RNA-seq counts enter as an `edgeR::DGEList`. Filter unexpressed and low-count
genes before fitting. For an ordinary model, mixedcirc uses `limma::voom()`.
For repeated measurements, it estimates voom-style mean-variance precision
weights with its own mixed-model implementation and then passes those weights
to the feature-wise circadian models. This pathway does not depend on the
`variancePartition` package.

```{r rnaseq, eval=requireNamespace("edgeR", quietly=TRUE)}
set.seed(41)
rna_counts <- matrix(
  stats::rnbinom(8 * nrow(sim$meta_input), mu = 80, size = 8),
  nrow = 8,
  dimnames = list(paste0("gene_", 1:8), NULL)
)
dge <- edgeR::DGEList(rna_counts)
dge <- edgeR::calcNormFactors(dge)
keep <- edgeR::filterByExpr(dge, group = sim$meta_input$group)
dge <- dge[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]

rna_fit <- mixedcirc_detect(
  dge,
  sim$meta_input,
  time = "time",
  group = "group",
  id = "id",
  lm_method = "lme",
  random_effect_type = "mesor"
)

head(mixedcirc_results(rna_fit, "estimates"))
```

Constant genes cannot provide a mean-variance relationship and should be
removed during filtering. The transformed values and observation weights used
for each successful fit are retained in its experimental design.

## Paired RRBS and BS-seq counts

Paired methylation input has two consecutive rows per biological observation:
the methylated count followed by the unmethylated count. `meta_input` still has
one row per biological observation. A unique `replicate_id` identifies each
pair. `mixedcirc_rrbs_qc()` validates this layout and summarizes coverage
without reordering or filtering the data.

```{r rrbs-qc, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
rrbs <- mixedcirc_simulate_data(
  n_subjects_per_group = 3,
  n_timepoints = 6,
  n_features = 4,
  groups = c("A", "B"),
  rrbs = TRUE,
  seed = 53
)

rrbs_qc <- mixedcirc_rrbs_qc(
  rrbs$data_input,
  rrbs$meta_input,
  replicate_id = "replicate_id",
  min_coverage = 8
)
rrbs_qc
mixedcirc_plot_rrbs_qc(rrbs_qc, type = "feature_coverage")
```

The paired model conditions on coverage through sample-specific terms and
estimates the rhythmic methylation effect on the methylated-count indicator.
Supply a positive weight matrix with the same paired dimensions, or request
internal weight estimation.

```{r rrbs-fit}
rrbs_fit <- mixedcirc_detect(
  rrbs$data_input,
  rrbs$meta_input,
  time = "time",
  group = "group",
  id = "id",
  RRBS = TRUE,
  replicate_id = "replicate_id",
  obs_weights = rrbs$obs_weights,
  random_effect_type = "mesor"
)

head(mixedcirc_results(rrbs_fit, "estimates"))
```

The paired-count strategy follows Chen et al. (2017), *Differential methylation
analysis of reduced representation bisulfite sequencing experiments using
edgeR*, F1000Research, <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5747346/>.

For very large data already stored as a `methylKit::methylBaseDB`, the
experimental `mixedcirc_rrbs_voom_mixed()` function processes tabix-backed data
in chunks. It relies on methylKit's internal on-disk API, checks compatibility
at run time, and writes generated databases beside the input database. The
optional `mixed_circ_tss_calculation()` and `construct_introns()` functions
support BED/GFF annotation of methylation loci.

## Repeated-measures associations and lags

`mixedcirc_compare()` compares observed or fitted signals using directional
association models, Pearson correlation, or repeated-measures correlation.
`mixedcirc_add_lag()` creates the shifted signals used in these comparisons.

Lags count positions after observations are ordered by time within the selected
subject or group. They are not clock-time units. With irregular sampling, one
lag step can represent different elapsed times and should not be described as a
fixed number of hours.

```{r lag-comparison}
lag_sim <- mixedcirc_simulate_data(
  n_subjects_per_group = 4,
  n_timepoints = 8,
  n_features = 2,
  groups = c("A", "B"),
  cross_lag_spec = list(
    list(from = 1, to = 2, lag = 1, beta = 1)
  ),
  seed = 61
)

lag_fit <- mixedcirc_detect(
  lag_sim$data_input,
  lag_sim$meta_input,
  time = "time",
  group = "group",
  id = "id"
)

mixedcirc_compare(
  lag_fit[[1]],
  lag_fit[[2]],
  lags = -2:2,
  analysis = "pearson"
)$results
```

These are association analyses, not tests of causal direction. Searching
several lags on the same data is exploratory; the returned p-values are not
adjusted across candidate lags.

## Large feature panels

`ncores` controls feature-parallel fitting. mixedcirc restores the caller's
existing `future` plan when fitting finishes, including after an error.

Set `store_models = FALSE` when only estimates, tests, and diagnostics are
needed. This reduces object size, but interpolation, subject-level prediction,
and bootstrap procedures require retained model objects. By default one failed
feature stops the run. `on_error = "keep"` instead records the failure and
continues with the other features.

```{r high-throughput, eval=FALSE}
large_fit <- mixedcirc_detect(
  large_matrix,
  metadata,
  time = "time",
  group = "condition",
  id = "subject",
  ncores = 4,
  store_models = FALSE,
  on_error = "keep"
)

mixedcirc_results(large_fit, "diagnostics")
```

Review failed, non-converged, singular, or rank-deficient fits before drawing
biological conclusions. `mixedcirc_adjust()` remains available for adding
adjusted columns to the original wide feature results, while
`mixedcirc_results()` and `mixedcirc_contrasts()` provide correction directly
in their analysis-ready tables.

## Experimental multi-omics integration

`mixedcirc_integrate()` performs supervised sparse generalized canonical
correlation analysis across two or more omics blocks. The time and optional
group design are part of the component-learning procedure. Consequently,
testing the learned scores against the same design in the same samples is not
independent confirmatory evidence. Use the scores for exploration, or validate
them with independent data or resampling that repeats the complete integration
workflow.

```{r integration, eval=FALSE}
blocks <- list(
  transcript = transcript_matrix,
  metabolite = metabolite_matrix
)

integrated <- mixedcirc_integrate(
  blocks,
  meta_input = metadata,
  time = "time",
  group = "condition",
  id = "subject"
)

scores <- mixedcirc_getscore(integrated, type = "average")
```

## Practical checklist

Before fitting, confirm that sample order matches the metadata, time is numeric,
subject and group labels are correct, the chosen period matches the scientific
question, and count data have been filtered appropriately. For RRBS, run the
paired-count QC first. After fitting, inspect diagnostics, adjust p-values
across features, use direct contrasts for group differences, and report effect
sizes and uncertainty alongside significance thresholds.
